clue.text: Half-boot was examined outside — poor footwear

indicators.note: outside tells us the exam word goes around the other piece, enclosing it

parts.note: someone who sat an exam was examined, so this gives sat

indicators.note: half of the word boot means only its front part is used here

explanation.surface: A complaint about shoddy half-boots that failed an inspection.
explanation.walkthrough: 'outside' puts SAT round BO, the first half of 'boot'. A sabot is a clog carved from wood, so it is rough, cheap footwear.
explanation.definitionFit: A sabot is a wooden clog worn by peasants, the humblest sort of shoe.

clue.text: Incidental information. Very marginal perhaps

explanation.surface: A note that a fact is peripheral, perhaps barely relevant.
explanation.walkthrough: The second definition is playful: a light on the side of a car or window is very much at the margin.
explanation.definitionFit: A side issue shedding indirect light on a subject; also a small lamp or window at the edge.

clue.text: Buffalo Bill's head is on this

indicators.note: a head is what comes first, so the opening letter of the word is taken

explanation.surface: Buffalo Bill's head appears on this item.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Buffalo Bill' runs together as the showman's name, but the definition is just 'Buffalo'.
explanation.definitionFit: The American bison is commonly called a buffalo.

clue.text: Ties broken, repaired within a decade

indicators.note: within says the second piece sits inside the first, which is broken open to receive it

parts.note: to repair to a place is to go there, so repaired means went

explanation.surface: Neckties torn and then mended over ten years.
explanation.walkthrough: 'broken' shows TIES split open, and 'within' puts WENT inside it. 'repaired' suggests mending but means went, as in repaired to the bar.
explanation.definitionFit: The twenties is the ten-year span from twenty to twenty-nine.

clue.text: Judge's informal greeting heard here — as is 7?

indicators.note: heard says the words are judged by how they sound when spoken

parts.note: a judge greeting the room casually might say hi, court

explanation.surface: A judge says a casual hello where cases are tried, and a printing term joins in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hi, court!' spoken sounds like the name of the court. 'as is 7?' adds a pun: a case heard in a superior court is an upper case, the answer to 7 down.
explanation.definitionFit: England's senior civil court is where a judge's cases are heard, the place meant by 'here'.

clue.text: Top, position kept by Kipling's man

annotationWithheld.why: Top, position kept by Kipling's man (4) for HEAR: no parse of 'Top position kept by Kipling's man' builds HEAR, and no blog or database gives one
annotationWithheld.clue: Top, position kept by Kipling's man

clue.text: Theatre transport terrific on straight maybe …

definitions.text: Theatre transport terrific on straight maybe

parts.words: Theatre transport terrific on straight maybe
parts.note: a fairground ride meant to frighten, and also the title of a famous straight play, one with no music

explanation.surface: A thrilling vehicle on a stage or a racetrack straight.
explanation.walkthrough: The Ghost Train is a 1920s stage thriller by Arnold Ridley; 'straight' means a straight play, not a musical, and 'terrific' is used in its old sense of terrifying.
explanation.definitionFit: A scary fairground ride through dark tunnels, and a classic stage comedy-thriller of that name.

clue.text: … but 'put in a tight spot where it ends

explanation.surface: Following the previous clue, trapping someone where the track turns.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis links back to 5 down: a straight ends at a bend.
explanation.definitionFit: To trap someone is to leave them with no way out; a bend in a road is where a straight stops.

clue.text: Used by printers throughout EEC — only starting in America

definitions.text: throughout EEC — only starting in America

explanation.surface: A typesetting style used fully in one acronym but only once in a country's name.
explanation.walkthrough: EEC is written all in capitals, while America has a capital only at the start.
explanation.definitionFit: Printers kept capital letters in the higher tray of type; EEC is all capitals, America has just one.

clue.text: Was trifling to the old, old, copper

parts.note: ye is an old way of writing the
d was the abbreviation for an old penny, a copper coin

explanation.surface: Someone wasting time with a mention of ancient coins.
explanation.walkthrough: D stood for the pre-1971 British penny (from Latin denarius), a copper coin.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who toyed with something played with it idly rather than seriously.

clue.text: Reckless speed, bad road, this sort of driver?

definitions.text: Reckless speed, bad road, this sort of driver?

indicators.note: bad suggests something gone wrong, so the letters of the two words are jumbled

explanation.surface: A tearaway motorist speeding down a poor road.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bad' is the anagram signal on SPEED and ROAD; the whole clue then describes the reckless outlaw a desperado is.
explanation.definitionFit: A desperado is a reckless, violent outlaw, the sort who drives too fast on bad roads.

clue.text: Work steadily again? That's the answer

parts.note: re- is the prefix meaning again
to ply a trade is to work at it steadily

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether doing a job steadily once more counts as a response.
explanation.definitionFit: A reply is a response given to a question or letter.

clue.text: Winning margin in point-to-point?

explanation.surface: A question about how races are won in amateur horse racing.
explanation.walkthrough: A point-to-point is a British amateur steeplechase; horses win by a length, and the distance from one point to another is also a length.
explanation.definitionFit: A horse's body-span is a common race margin, and the measured distance between two points is its extent.

clue.text: A pound in debt, at first 'e wasn't ready

indicators.note: at first says this letter is placed at the front of the rest

parts.note: dropped-aitch 'e is he, giving the letter E

indicators.note: in puts the pound inside the phrase for being in debt

parts.note: being in debt is being in the red, so the red supplies these letters
L is the abbreviation for a pound sterling, from Latin libra

explanation.surface: A Cockney admits he owed a pound and was caught unprepared.
explanation.walkthrough: L inside THE RED (debt) gives THELRED, with E in front. Ethelred the Unready was an English king, hence 'wasn't ready'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Anglo-Saxon king is remembered by the nickname 'the Unready', meaning poorly advised.

clue.text: Ailing, repeat cure?

indicators.note: ailing means sick or unwell, so the letters are disordered

explanation.surface: Asking whether a sick person should take the treatment again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ailing' rearranges REPEAT CURE, and the clue as a whole describes getting well again.
explanation.definitionFit: To recuperate is to recover health after illness, which a repeated cure aims at.

clue.text: No such fruit in the Garden of Eden

definitions.text: No such fruit in the Garden of Eden

parts.words: No such fruit in the Garden of Eden
parts.note: with only Adam and Eve there, nobody could be the unwanted third party on a couple's outing, which is this fruit's other sense

explanation.surface: A claim that a certain fruit never grew in Paradise.
explanation.walkthrough: To play the gooseberry is British slang for being the unwanted third person with a couple; Eden had only two people.
explanation.definitionFit: The green berry also names a third wheel tagging along with lovers, impossible with just two humans.

clue.text: Society's rejection of non-U music and art-so upsetting

indicators.note: upsetting means knocking over and disordering, so the letters are rearranged
non-U says the letter U is taken out of the word

explanation.surface: Snobbish disdain for lower-class music and art.
explanation.walkthrough: Non-U is British slang for not upper-class. Taking U from MUSIC leaves MSIC, rearranged with ART and SO.
explanation.definitionFit: Ostracism is exclusion from a group or community.

clue.text: Adventuress who placated Dracula?

indicators.note: someone placated has had their anger taken away, so the ire is removed

parts.note: Dracula is the most famous vampire

explanation.surface: A seductress who managed to calm the Count.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove IRE (anger) from VAMPIRE, as one 'placated' loses their ire.
explanation.definitionFit: A vamp is a woman who uses her charm to exploit men, an adventuress.

clue.text: 22 dn figures very much outfaced by these -

definitions.text: 22 dn figures very much outfaced by these

parts.words: 22 dn figures very much outfaced by these
parts.note: cube-shaped solids are outdone in faces by shapes with many sides, poly meaning many and the Greek root for face completing the word

explanation.surface: A remark that cubes are outnumbered in faces by other shapes.
explanation.walkthrough: 22 down is CUBIC; a cube has six faces, while these solids may have many more.
explanation.definitionFit: Solids with many flat faces have more sides than a cube.

clue.text: Didn't seek all-out effort from team, it's said

definitions.text: Didn't seek all-out effort from team

explanation.surface: A captain who did not demand the most from his side.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a captain who declares ends the batting innings before all the batsmen are out.
explanation.definitionFit: Ending a cricket innings before every batsman is dismissed; also announced or stated.

clue.text: North American bear seen in early totem-pole

indicators.note: seen in early says the letters sit inside the opening part of the following word

explanation.surface: A bear spotted on an old carved totem pole.
explanation.walkthrough: The opening letters of 'totem' give the word. 'bear' looks like the animal but means carry, and tote is chiefly American.
explanation.definitionFit: To tote is to carry, a usage chiefly American.

clue.text: Clanger that's singularly disastrous

parts.note: a clanger is a bell, and this one at Lloyd's of London was struck once for news of a lost ship

explanation.surface: A gaffe that is uniquely catastrophic.
explanation.walkthrough: A clanger is British slang for a blunder. The Lutine Bell hangs at Lloyd's of London, the insurance market, and was rung once for a ship lost, twice for good news.
explanation.definitionFit: The salvaged ship's bell at Lloyd's announced losses with a single stroke.

clue.text: Disgrace to be drunk

parts.note: a blot on one's name is a disgrace

explanation.surface: It is shameful to be inebriated.
explanation.definitionFit: Blotto is British slang for very drunk.

clue.text: Foolish fellows cancelling ad in dailies

indicators.note: cancelling says the advert is struck out of the longer word

parts.note: a daily is British for a cleaning woman, a charlady
ad is taken as written

explanation.surface: Silly men pulling an advertisement from the newspapers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dailies' looks like newspapers but means daily cleaning women, charladies; take out AD. Charlies is British slang for fools.
explanation.definitionFit: A charlie is British slang for a silly person.

clue.text: Youngster gets one hundred in such form after square cuts?

definitions.text: in such form after square cuts?

parts.note: a cub is a young animal or a youngster
I is the Roman numeral for one
C is the Roman numeral for a hundred

explanation.surface: A young cricketer scores a century with square cuts.
explanation.walkthrough: The square cut is a cricket stroke, but here cutting into squares gives dice-shaped pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Cutting into squares in three dimensions produces cube-shaped pieces.

clue.text: Almost black, he contrived to turn white

indicators.note: contrived means made up or arranged artificially, so the letters are rearranged
almost tells us to stop the word one letter short of its end

parts.note: black is taken as written before the trim

explanation.surface: Something nearly black is somehow made to go white.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Almost' drops the K of BLACK; 'contrived' rearranges BLAC and HE.
explanation.definitionFit: To bleach something is to whiten it by removing colour.

clue.text: Besides, being split is an improvement.

parts.note: an gives the letter a as the article
a gain is an improvement

explanation.surface: Moreover, being divided is a step forward.
explanation.walkthrough: 'being split' says the answer splits into two words, A GAIN.
explanation.definitionFit: Again can mean besides or moreover, introducing a further point.

clue.text: Exact copy of Cook's revolver

explanation.surface: A cook's firearm is a perfect duplicate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'revolver' looks like a gun but is the rotating rod for roasting meat.
explanation.definitionFit: The spit of someone is their double; a rotating skewer turns meat over a fire.

clue.text: Put up, however.., with the Italian invasion

indicators.note: an invasion is one thing entering another, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: but and however both mean nevertheless
il is the Italian for the

explanation.surface: Something was erected, though Italy invaded.
explanation.walkthrough: IL ('the' in Italian) goes inside BUT.
explanation.definitionFit: Something put up has been constructed or erected.

clue.text: It shows union 'olds up the worker

parts.note: holds up means hampers, and with the h dropped as the apostrophe shows it becomes 'ampers
a worker is a hand, and with the h dropped it becomes 'and

explanation.surface: A Cockney complaint that something is delaying the labourer.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe in ''olds' tells you to drop each H: HAMPERS and HAND lose their H.
explanation.definitionFit: The & symbol stands for 'and', the word that joins things.

clue.text: Extremely vulgar general — couldn't be more so

explanation.surface: A crude army officer whose coarseness is unsurpassed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'general' looks like the army rank but is the adjective: common means general, and this is its most extreme form.
explanation.definitionFit: Most vulgar is the superlative of coarse; most widespread is the superlative of general or usual.

clue.text: Mobile type gets on and travels-back round

indicators.note: round says one piece goes about the other
travels back says the word is read in the opposite direction

parts.note: and is taken as written
on is taken as written

explanation.surface: A traveller on the move doubles back on itself.
explanation.walkthrough: 'travels-back' turns AND into DNA, which goes 'round' ON. The aria 'La donna è mobile' from Verdi's Rigoletto calls woman fickle.
explanation.definitionFit: Verdi's famous aria says 'la donna è mobile', woman is changeable, so she is the mobile type.
